slides.heading: Start with a controlled row
slides.body: A row and a light reverse fly are a manageable starting point.
slides.narration: For a manageable middle back workout, start with a row you can control and a light reverse fly. Keep your torso steady and record the setup so you can repeat it. This IZEM guide is an introductory strength example for healthy adults. If you have persistent pain or an injury, ask your healthcare professional which movements suit you. Stop an exercise that causes pain.

slides.heading: Choose equipment you can set up reliably
slides.body: Dumbbells, a cable station, a supported machine or a band.
slides.narration: Choose the row you can set up reliably. With dumbbells and an adjustable bench, a chest supported row is one option. A cable station or supported row machine can work too. At home, a seated band row is another choice. Inspect your band and follow the manufacturer's setup instructions. Do not improvise an anchor from unstable furniture. Record the bench angle, machine settings or band stretch.

slides.heading: Begin with a small session
slides.body: Warm up, then start with one controlled set of each movement.
slides.narration: Warm up with a few minutes of easy activity and rehearse the row with light resistance. The article's starting example is one set of twelve to fifteen controlled rows and one set of twelve to fifteen light incline reverse flyes. Rest about two minutes after the row, and allow enough recovery to move steadily. Choose resistance that makes the last repetitions challenging while you can still control them. You do not need to force a failed repetition.

slides.heading: Keep the row repeatable
slides.body: Avoid swinging your torso to finish the pull.
slides.narration: For a seated row, sit with knees slightly bent and your back in a comfortable neutral position. Draw your elbows back beside your ribs without swinging your torso. Pause briefly and return slowly. Let your shoulder blades move together without forcing a hard pinch or tensing your neck. Your arms will work too. Check the movement you can observe instead of judging the set only by where you feel it.

slides.heading: Use light resistance for reverse flyes
slides.body: Keep your chest supported and lower slowly.
slides.narration: For an incline reverse fly, use light dumbbells and a stable bench with the backrest at forty five to sixty degrees. Keep your chest supported and feet planted. With a slight bend in the elbows, raise your arms out toward shoulder height within a comfortable range. Lower slowly. Reduce the load if you cannot maintain the position. Ask a gym instructor to check an unfamiliar setup.

slides.heading: Record setup, resistance and repetitions
slides.body: Compare the same movement before adding weight.
slides.narration: Record your row variation, setup, resistance, controlled repetitions and what stopped the set. If twelve controlled repetitions become fifteen at the same resistance and movement, that is a useful comparison. Once extra repetitions feel manageable, try a small resistance increase and build back up. With a band, record a change in band strength or starting stretch. Change one variable at a time.

slides.heading: Fit the work into your existing plan
slides.body: Count the rows you already do and allow recovery.
slides.narration: Count rows and reverse flyes already in your plan before adding more. Leave a full day before training the same muscles again, and keep training the rest of your body. A second row set is one possible next step when the session is manageable and you are recovering well. The complete guide includes equipment choices, linked exercise demonstrations and a copyable training log. Read it at youraicoach dot life slash blog slash middle back workouts.
